title: Weak Value Comparison Degrades to 1/n on the Needle Profile
body_html:
Weak Value Comparison Degrades to 1/n on the Needle Profile

Counterexample (welfare_eq_zero_needle_last). Consider the sample-then-threshold variant of the online single-item auction (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) that observes the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ arrivals, then accepts any later bidder whose value is at least the maximum value observed in the observe phase. On the needle profile (one bidder with value $M$, the rest with value $0$) this rule achieves expected welfare only $(1/n) \cdot \max v$, which is not a constant competitive ratio.

This complements the strict-comparison counterexample (Strict Value Comparison Breaks the Competitive Guarantee), which gives welfare $= 0$ outright. Weak comparison avoids that extreme failure but introduces a subtler one: the threshold is too permissive at value ties, letting the wrong bidder win.

Construction

Fix $M > 0$ and set

$$ v = (M,\, 0,\, 0,\, \ldots,\, 0), \qquad n \ge 2. $$

One needle bidder has value $M$; the remaining $n - 1$ haystack bidders have value $0$. The auction observes the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ arrivals (rejecting them all), records the maximum value $p$ seen during this phase, then admits any later bidder whose value satisfies $p \le v$.

Case analysis over the needle's arrival position

Under a uniformly random permutation, the needle bidder is equally likely to occupy any of the $n$ positions.

Case 1: needle in the observe phase (position $k < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$).

The recorded maximum is $\ge M$, so the threshold is $\ge M$. Every phase-2 bidder has value $0$, and $M \le 0$ is false. Nobody is admitted. Welfare $= 0$.

Case 2: needle in phase 2, but not first (position $k > \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$).

All phase-1 bidders have value $0$, so the threshold is $0$. The first phase-2 bidder is a haystack bidder with value $0$, and the weak test $0 \le 0$ succeeds. They are admitted immediately with welfare $= 0$. The needle never gets a chance to bid.

Case 3: needle is first in phase 2 (position $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$).

The threshold is $0$ and the needle's value $M$ clears it. Admitted. Welfare $= M$.

Expected welfare is $M/n$

Exactly one of $n$ equally likely positions delivers welfare $M$; all others deliver welfare $0$. Hence

$$ \mathbb{E}[\text{welfare}] = \frac{1}{n} \cdot M = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \max_i v_i. $$

For any constant $c > 0$, choosing $n > 1/c$ gives $\mathbb{E}[\text{welfare}] < c \cdot \max v$, so weak comparison achieves no constant competitive ratio on this profile family.

Remarks

Why the proper sample-then-threshold auction avoids this

The single-item auction's acceptance rule (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) attaches an identity tag to the threshold. The sample-then-threshold auction (Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive) sets that tag to the largest identity $g_{\max}$ observed in phase 1, so the acceptance test becomes "value strictly above $p$, or value equal to $p$ and identity at least $g_{\max}$".

In Case 2, every later haystack bidder $j$ has value $0$ and identity $g_j < g_{\max}$ (since $g_{\max}$ was the maximum over all phase-1 identities, which included $j$'s peers). The test then fails on the identity tag and the haystack bidder is rejected. Rejection continues until the needle arrives, clears the value threshold strictly ($0 < M$), and is admitted with welfare $M$.

On the favourable event (probability $\ge 1/4$, when the lex-argmax sits in phase 2 and the lex-second sits in phase 1), the lex rule rejects every haystack bidder and admits the needle, giving welfare $= M$. The overall guarantee is $\ge (1/4) \cdot M$.

The mechanism of failure

The root cause is that weak comparison cannot distinguish between a haystack bidder matching the threshold by coincidence and the needle bidder genuinely exceeding it. When the threshold is $0$ and all haystack values are $0$, the test $0 \le 0$ is vacuously true — the first phase-2 arrival wins regardless of their value.

The identity tag of the lexicographic threshold breaks this degeneracy: at the threshold price, the bidder also has to clear an identity tag derived from the observed maximum. This filters out haystack bidders whose only "qualification" is matching a zero value threshold, which is the design motivation behind the single-item auction's lex rule (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction).

Summary table

Acceptance rule Needle profile welfare Constant competitive?
Strict $p < v$ $0$ always No (Strict Value Comparison Breaks the Competitive Guarantee)
Weak $p \le v$ $M/n$ in expectation No (this counterexample)
Lex (price + identity) $\ge M/4$ in expectation Yes (Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive)

Lean formalization

In EconCSLib, the weak variant is the auction Online.Auction.WeakComparison.auction. It is obtained from the generic SingleItemAuction B F template by setting the threshold's identity component to ⊥ : B (under [OrderBot B]); the acceptance test threshold h ≤ ↑(toLex (v, b)) then degenerates to $p \le v$ on first components, since ⊥ ≤ b' holds for every $b'$.

The needle-profile failure is the chain of two lemmas maxPairFold_fst_zero (in the Case-2 sub-trajectory the phase-1 history has identically zero values, so the recorded value threshold is $0$) and welfare_eq_zero_needle_last (once the threshold is $0$, the first phase-2 arrival is admitted with value $0$). The proper sample-then-threshold auction uses Online.Auction.SampleThenThreshold.auction, whose maxPairFold carries both the running maximum value and the running maximum identity into the threshold's identity component.

References

  • [Roughgarden 2016, Lecture 2, Problem 2.1(c)] Tim Roughgarden, Twenty Lectures on Algorithmic Game Theory, Cambridge University Press. Random-order (secretary-style) analysis (stated for distinct values, which excludes the needle profile).
